summary: Describes using entropy labels to improve load balancing across MPLS networks. It defines the concept, explains why such labels are useful, and lists properties that allow maximal benefit. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: An MPLS ingress router can add a label derived from packet fields so later routers can distribute flows across paths. A marker before that label tells routers that it is for balancing, not forwarding.

subtitle: An extra MPLS label carries flow variation so transit routers can balance traffic without inspecting the payload.

tldr.problem: Transit MPLS routers may not be able to identify useful packet fields for load balancing, so traffic can be spread unevenly across equal-cost paths.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress router hashes suitable packet fields and places the result in an entropy label. A reserved Entropy Label Indicator before it tells routers how to interpret the next label.
tldr.outcome: Entropy labels improve load-balancing inputs at the cost of two labels in the stack. RFC 6790 updates RFC 3031, RFC 3107, RFC 3209, and RFC 5036, and has been updated by later RFCs.

today: RFC 6790 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3031, RFC 3107, RFC 3209, and RFC 5036. It has been updated by RFC 7274, RFC 7447, and RFC 8012.

sections.title: Why MPLS Needs More Load-Balancing Information
sections.content:
Load balancing can spread traffic over multiple paths, but packets from one flow should use the same path to avoid jitter, latency, and reordering. Routers choose a path from packet fields such as addresses, protocol, and ports.

An MPLS transit router may not know which payload it carries. If it hashes only labels, many different flows can produce the same input and traffic may be distributed poorly. The ingress router has more information before MPLS encapsulation, so RFC 6790 places its flow hash in an additional label.
sections.plainLanguage: The first router can see packet details that later MPLS routers may not see. It adds a label based on those details so later routers have a better input for balancing flows.

sections.title: The Entropy Label and Its Marker
sections.content:
An entropy label is not used to forward the packet and is not signaled as an ordinary forwarding label. Its purpose is to add variation to the label stack for load balancing. The ingress generates it from load-balancing information, and its value must not be in the reserved label range.

Because an ingress creates this label while application labels are allocated downstream, an egress needs a clear way to distinguish them. The RFC places an Entropy Label Indicator (ELI), reserved value 7, immediately before each entropy label.

This approach adds the ELI and entropy label to the stack. The RFC chooses this increase in stack depth rather than requiring extra forwarding and signaling state for multiple equivalent labels.
sections.plainLanguage: The entropy label carries a hash result for balancing, not a forwarding destination. A reserved marker immediately before it tells the egress how to recognize the pair.

sections.title: Where the Label Pair Fits
sections.content:
Entropy labels are associated with MPLS tunnels rather than individual applications. A tunnel can carry different services, and each layer of a tunnel hierarchy can make its own choice about using entropy labels.

The pair is inserted in the label stack near the tunnel label. The entropy label itself is not used for forwarding; the marker identifies it to routers that understand the feature. An ingress must not insert the pair for a tunnel unless the egress has signaled that it can process entropy labels there.

The approach is also useful with pseudowires, but RFC 6790 focuses on tunnels and other MPLS applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The label pair belongs to a tunnel, which may carry several applications. The egress must first signal that it can recognize and remove the pair.

sections.title: Ingress, Transit, and Egress Processing
sections.content:
The ingress identifies the application and hashes appropriate packet fields. If the egress has advertised support for the tunnel, the ingress pushes the tunnel label, ELI, and entropy label in the required order.

A transit router may leave its forwarding behavior unchanged. If it recognizes the ELI, it may balance using the following label; otherwise, it should use as much of the label stack as it can. Reserved labels must not be used as hash inputs.

The egress removes the tunnel label and, when present, the ELI and entropy label before processing the remaining packet. It must ignore the entropy label's TTL. A penultimate-hop router needs no change, although it may remove the pair if that does not impair its next-hop balancing.
sections.plainLanguage: The ingress adds the marked label after checking the egress capability. Transit routers can use it to balance traffic, and the egress removes the pair before continuing normal processing.

sections.title: Signaling Egress Capability
sections.content:
An egress signals its Entropy Label Capability for a tunnel. The capability can differ by direction, so each direction is signaled separately. An egress must be ready to remove an entropy-label pair even when penultimate-hop popping is used.

The RFC defines signaling extensions for LDP, BGP, and RSVP-TE. LDP uses an ELC TLV; BGP uses an optional transitive path attribute; RSVP-TE uses an ELC flag in the LSP attributes. Each protocol carries the information in its own control message format.

For multicast LSPs, entropy labels may help on bundled links even though multicast LSPs typically do not use ECMP. Detailed multicast signaling and processing are left to a future document.
sections.plainLanguage: The egress tells the ingress whether it can handle the label pair for a tunnel. LDP, BGP, and RSVP-TE each carry that capability differently.

sections.title: Operations and Security
sections.content:
The RFC updates LSP traceroute so that a value from the range used to select a path is placed in the entropy label. This lets the test follow the selected path without requiring deep packet inspection, although an implementation may still inspect packets if it does so consistently.

Entropy labels do not apply to MPLS-TP because that profile does not use ECMP. The RFC says the signaling does not introduce new security vulnerabilities to LDP, BGP, or RSVP-TE.

If the label is calculated only from packet headers, the hash could help build a wiretapping interface. An implementation may add another input, such as a random value. If capability signaling is absent, the ingress falls back to forwarding without entropy labels.
sections.plainLanguage: Path tests can put their chosen path value in the entropy label. If capability is missing, routers use their existing behavior; implementations can also add an input to make labels harder to predict.
